t_acad.t: The Secret Life of Sleep in Animals
x: Almost all animals studied so far show some form of sleep, but the way they sleep varies enormously. Some birds and dolphins can rest one half of their brain at a time, keeping the other half alert. This allows dolphins to keep swimming and surface to breathe, and helps birds watch for predators.

The amount of sleep also differs widely between species. Large plant-eating animals such as giraffes and elephants may sleep only a few hours a day, possibly because they need to spend most of their time eating low-energy food. In contrast, some small animals that eat energy-rich food, such as bats, may sleep for more than eighteen hours.

Despite these differences, scientists believe sleep must have important functions, since it exists across so many species even though sleeping animals are vulnerable to attack. Current theories suggest that sleep helps to save energy, repair the body and process memories.
q: What is the passage mainly about?
How and why sleep differs among animals
Why can dolphins keep swimming while they sleep?
They rest one half of their brain at a time.
Some birds and dolphins can rest one half of their brain at a time, keeping the other half alert.
According to the passage, why might giraffes sleep so little?
They need to spend most of their time eating low-energy food.
possibly because they need to spend most of their time eating low-energy food
The word "vulnerable" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
sleeping animals are vulnerable to attack
Why do scientists believe sleep has important functions?
It exists in many species despite being risky.
All animals sleep the same amount.
since it exists across so many species even though sleeping animals are vulnerable to attack

x: Today I'd like to look at a behaviour we all share but rarely think about: yawning. For a long time, people believed we yawn because our bodies need more oxygen. However, experiments have shown that breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning.

A more recent theory suggests that yawning helps to cool the brain. When we yawn, we take in a large amount of air, which may lower the temperature of blood flowing to the head. Supporting this idea, studies have found that people yawn less often when the air around them is very hot.
Finally, yawning is contagious: seeing or even reading about someone yawning can make us yawn. Some researchers think this may be connected to empathy, our ability to share other people's feelings.
q: What is the talk mainly about?
How the brain works during sleep
What did experiments show about the oxygen theory?
Extra oxygen does not reduce yawning.
Yawning increases oxygen in the blood.
People yawn more in hot air.
experiments have shown that breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning
What evidence supports the brain-cooling theory?
People yawn less when the air is very hot.
People yawn more when they are hungry.
people yawn less often when the air around them is very hot
What do some researchers connect contagious yawning with?
Some researchers think this may be connected to empathy

i_read.t: The Return of the Night Train
x: A. In the 1990s and 2000s, many European night trains were withdrawn as cheap flights became popular and operators struggled to make a profit. Travellers could fly across the continent in a couple of hours, often for less than the price of a train ticket.

B. In recent years, however, night trains have made a comeback. Growing concern about the environmental impact of flying has encouraged many travellers to choose rail, which produces far lower emissions per passenger on most routes. Several new routes have opened, connecting cities such as Vienna, Berlin, Paris and Amsterdam.

C. Supporters point out that night trains also save time and money, as passengers travel while they sleep and do not need to pay for a hotel. Nevertheless, tickets for private sleeping cabins can still be expensive, and demand on popular routes often exceeds the number of available seats.
q: Night trains were withdrawn partly because of competition from cheap flights.
many European night trains were withdrawn as cheap flights became popular
Rail produces higher emissions per passenger than flying on most routes.
rail, which produces far lower emissions per passenger on most routes
The new route between Vienna and Paris is the most popular in Europe.
(The text lists cities but does not say which route is the most popular.)
Which heading best fits paragraph B?
A revival driven by environmental concern
The high cost of sleeping cabins
In recent years, however, night trains have made a comeback.
What problem with night trains is mentioned in paragraph C?
Demand is often higher than the number of seats.
demand on popular routes often exceeds the number of available seats

x: Today's lecture is about chocolate, which has a much longer history than most people realise.

The cacao tree is native to Central and South America, and evidence suggests that people there were using cacao more than three thousand years ago. However, they did not eat it as a sweet bar. Instead, they made a bitter drink, often flavoured with chilli.
Cacao beans were so valuable that the Aztecs even used them as a form of money.
When cacao reached Europe in the sixteenth century, sugar was added to make the drink sweeter, and it became fashionable among the rich.
It was only in the nineteenth century, with new industrial machines, that solid chocolate bars became cheap enough for ordinary people to buy.
q: Where is the cacao tree originally from?
The cacao tree is native to Central and South America
they made a bitter drink, often flavoured with chilli
What did the Aztecs use cacao beans for?
the Aztecs even used them as a form of money
What was added to the drink in Europe?
sugar was added to make the drink sweeter
What made chocolate bars cheap for ordinary people?
New industrial machines in the nineteenth century
Lower taxes in the sixteenth century
It was only in the nineteenth century, with new industrial machines, that solid chocolate bars became cheap enough
